evidence.title: Peri-LN: Revisiting Normalization Layer in the Transformer Architecture (Kim et al., ICML 2025)
evidence.quote: "we pre-trained each model with five different training seeds" (400M/1.5B/3.2B, 30B tokens each); Appendix G.4 on swapping RMSNorm for LayerNorm at 400M: "We observe no notable difference between using RMSNorm and LayerNorm", citing OLMo 2's identical finding.
evidence.what_it_shows: Five-seed, drop-in LN vs RMSNorm swap at 400M in a decoder LM: a null. Parity, not a win.

evidence.title: Do Transformer Modifications Transfer Across Implementations and Applications? (Narang et al., EMNLP 2021)
evidence.quote: "To capture the inter-run variance on these models, we run each model 5 times for 65,536 steps (1/8th of the total pre-training steps). We report the mean and standard deviation of the loss" - RMS Norm 2.167+/-0.008 vs Vanilla (LayerNorm) 2.182+/-0.005 at 223M, all hyperparameters held constant; final single-run loss 1.821 vs 1.838.
evidence.what_it_shows: The only multi-run evidence for a quality WIN: ~2 sigma at 1/8 budget, T5-style encoder-decoder, no LR retune per variant.

evidence.title: 2 OLMo 2 Furious (OLMo team, 2024/2025)
evidence.quote: "Our ablations show no difference between the two, so we switch back to RMSNorm" (non-parametric LayerNorm vs RMSNorm, 7B-class runs; seeds not stated).
evidence.what_it_shows: Large-scale practitioner null; the switch was made for library/hardware reasons, not quality.

evidence.title: nanogpt-from-scratch paired-seed ablation study (unrefereed GitHub report)
evidence.quote: 51.2M params, 8 layers x 512, 524M tokens per arm, 3 seeds per arm, baseline seed spread 0.0043; norm-rmsnorm arm: +0.0007 +/- 0.0021 val loss, classed "Noise" (per-seed deltas straddle zero).
evidence.what_it_shows: A nano-scale (51M) three-seed matched-budget null for LN vs RMSNorm; essentially the proposed test at 1/4 the seeds.

gap: Only a tighter null: a 12-seed nano run would add sign-per-seed at 10-60M, but the 3-seed 51M null, the 5-seed 400M null and the 7B null already bracket the scale range; low expected information unless paired with the gpt2 (post-norm-era) vs llama family split.
notes: Our prior was wrong in one respect: there IS a controlled multi-seed comparison (Peri-LN, 5 seeds, 400M-3.2B, appendix G.4) and it is a null, not a win. The verdict is SOLID for the 'matches' half of the claim; the 'beats' half rests on Narang's ~2-sigma 1/8-budget result and on no LR retune, so 'beats' should be dropped from the claim. The speed half is real but small (~6% throughput at 124M in nanoGPT-Valkyrie; T5's original 7-9% figure came from a naive two-pass TF LayerNorm). Pre-LN and pre-RMSNorm are provably near-equivalent (Jiang et al. 2023, arXiv:2305.14858), which is why nulls are expected; if the team runs this at all, the only interesting arm is post-norm placement where the mean-centring might matter.

evidence.title: On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture (Xiong et al., ICML 2020)
evidence.quote: IWSLT14/WMT14/BERT-base; Pre-LN without warmup reaches "comparable final performances but use much less training time" than Post-LN with warmup; the ten-seed repetition is used only for the gradient-norm-at-init verification, not for final-loss comparison.
evidence.what_it_shows: The origin paper claims speed and equal final quality, not better final quality; the multi-seed part is the theory check.

evidence.title: Understanding the Difficulty of Training Transformers (Liu et al., EMNLP 2020; Admin)
evidence.quote: "when Post-LN converges, it outperforms Pre-LN in 7 out of 8 settings" (15-configuration grid); WMT14 En-De 6L-6L BLEU Post-LN 27.80 vs Pre-LN 27.27; Post-LN fails at 12L and 18L. IWSLT numbers carry +/- (e.g. 35.64+/-0.23) but seed count is not stated. No language-modelling experiment.
evidence.what_it_shows: Controlled MT evidence that post-norm is better at convergence when it converges: the 'post-norm is dead' half is contradicted at shallow depth, but only for MT.

evidence.title: Mix-LN: Unleashing the Power of Deeper Layers by Combining Pre-LN and Post-LN (Li et al., 2024/2025)
evidence.quote: LLaMA-style LMs on C4: Post-LN vs Pre-LN perplexity 35.18 vs 34.77 (71M), 26.95 vs 26.78 (130M), 1409 vs 21.92 (250M), 1411 vs 18.65 (1B); "identical configurations except for the normalization"; no seeds, no per-variant LR tuning (1e-3 for <=250M).
evidence.what_it_shows: Single-seed LM evidence: post-norm slightly worse at 71-130M and diverges at 250M+ under a shared LR; confounded by no per-arm LR/warmup tuning.

evidence.title: Peri-LN: Revisiting Normalization Layer in the Transformer Architecture (Kim et al., ICML 2025)
evidence.quote: "we pre-trained each model with five different training seeds", LR swept 1e-4 to 5e-3; 400M: Post-LN loss 7.46 vs Pre-LN 3.43 vs Peri-LN 3.34; 1.5B: 5.38 vs 3.29 vs 3.18; 3.2B: 4.43 vs 3.20 vs 3.11; Pre-LN diverged more often than Peri-LN in early training.
evidence.what_it_shows: Five-seed, LR-swept LM evidence at 400M-3.2B that post-norm is far worse (effectively fails) and that pre-norm is itself the less stable of the two modern placements.

gap: Nobody has run pre vs post placement for a decoder LM at 10-60M with per-arm warmup/LR tuning and seeds: the MT-derived 'post-norm wins when it converges' (Admin, Nguyen & Salazar 2019 on WMT En-De 27.58 vs 26.83) has never been checked for language modelling at any scale with a variance estimate, and the LM evidence at 71-130M (Mix-LN) is single-seed with a shared LR.
notes: Our prior is right that the post-norm-with-warmup advantage is real and rarely repeated, but it is MT-only (Admin, Nguyen & Salazar 2019 arXiv:1910.05895). For LMs the controlled evidence (Peri-LN, 5 seeds) says post-norm collapses from 400M up even with an LR sweep, so the claim is scale- and task-dependent rather than settled. Also note the frame has moved: the live 2025 question is Pre-LN vs Peri-LN (both beat Post-LN), and OLMo 2 uses a reordered ('post-norm on the sublayer output') layout with QK-norm. A nano test should include warmup as a factor, as proposed, because that is exactly the confound the LM papers do not vary.

evidence.title: GLU Variants Improve Transformer (Shazeer 2020)
evidence.quote: "For each model architecture, we also trained four models for a shorter period (65,536 steps) to measure inter-run variability"; GLU variants "reduce the hidden layer to d_ff=2048" (from 3072) to match parameters and ops; log-perplexity at 65k steps: ReLU 1.997 (0.005), GELU 1.983 (0.005), SwiGLU 1.944 (0.010), GEGLU 1.942 (0.004); at 524k steps ReLU 1.677, GELU 1.679, SwiGLU 1.636.
evidence.what_it_shows: Parameter-matched, four-run variance estimate, 12-layer d768 T5 encoder-decoder: the SwiGLU gain (~0.04 nats) is ~8x the run-to-run std.

evidence.title: Do Transformer Modifications Transfer Across Implementations and Applications? (Narang et al., EMNLP 2021)
evidence.quote: 223M params, 5 runs at 1/8 budget: SwiGLU 2.127+/-0.003 vs GeLU 2.179+/-0.003 vs Vanilla ReLU 2.182+/-0.005; final loss 1.789 vs 1.838; SwiGLU/GeGLU among the few modifications that "consistently improved performance".
evidence.what_it_shows: Independent replication in the same family with a 5-run variance estimate: a ~15-sigma effect at matched parameters.

evidence.title: What Language Model to Train if You Have One Million GPU Hours? (Le Scao et al., 2022)
evidence.quote: 1.3B decoder-only ablations on 112B tokens, d_ff=8/3 d_model to match compute: SwiGLU 42.95 vs GELU 42.79 average EAI-harness score; single run per ablation, no variance reported.
evidence.what_it_shows: Decoder-only, 1.3B: direction preserved but the downstream delta is tiny and single-seed.

evidence.title: nanogpt-from-scratch paired-seed ablation study (unrefereed GitHub report)
evidence.quote: 51.2M params, 3 seeds, 524M tokens: mlp-swiglu -0.0341 +/- 0.0035 val loss vs GELU, every seed agreed in direction; but "at 512 width, the 2/3 scaling for SwiGLU produces 1536 hidden units" vs 2048, i.e. ~12% more MLP parameters in the SwiGLU arm.
evidence.what_it_shows: Nano-scale 3-seed sign agreement for SwiGLU over GELU; the parameter match is slightly off in SwiGLU's favour.

gap: A 12-seed exact-parameter-match run at 10-60M would only add the sign-per-seed at nano scale (already 3/3 at 51M with a small param mismatch) and the loss-delta band; the open questions are elsewhere: whether the gap shrinks with scale (Scao's 1.3B downstream delta is ~0) and whether the GLU gain is gating rather than Swish (ReLU^2 and xIELU beat SwiGLU at 1.1-1.3B).
notes: Our prior 'one seed per variant' is wrong: Shazeer trained four repeats per variant at 1/8 budget and reported std, and Narang repeated it with five. The 'no explanation' line is real but the effect is well replicated at 220M encoder-decoder, 1.3B decoder and 51M decoder (3 seeds). What is NOT established is that SwiGLU is the best activation: xIELU (arXiv:2411.13010; 1.1B, 126B tokens: SwiGLU 2.353+/-0.004 vs ReLU^2 2.337+/-0.004 vs xIELU 2.323+/-0.004), Primer's squared ReLU (arXiv:2109.08668, multi-run at 35M) and ReLU^2 Wins (arXiv:2402.03804; 1.3B: SwiGLU 50.53 vs ReLU^2 50.48 vs ReGLU 50.36) all show non-gated squared ReLU at parity or better. If the team runs an activation panel, add ReLU^2 as an arm; that is where the literature is thin at nano scale with seeds.

evidence.title: GLU Variants Improve Transformer (Shazeer 2020)
evidence.quote: Four-run variance at 65k steps: FFN-ReLU 1.997 (0.005) vs FFN-GELU 1.983 (0.005) vs FFN-Swish 1.994 (0.003); at 524k steps ReLU 1.677 vs GELU 1.679 vs Swish 1.683 (matched d_ff=3072).
evidence.what_it_shows: ReLU vs GELU at full budget is a dead heat (ReLU marginally lower); at 1/8 budget GELU leads by ~2-3 std.

evidence.title: Do Transformer Modifications Transfer Across Implementations and Applications? (Narang et al., EMNLP 2021)
evidence.quote: 5 runs at 1/8 budget: Vanilla (ReLU) 2.182+/-0.005 vs GeLU 2.179+/-0.003; final loss 1.838 vs 1.838; SGLUE 71.66 vs 75.79 (single fine-tune runs).
evidence.what_it_shows: Pretraining loss identical within noise at 223M; the only GELU advantage is on single-run downstream fine-tuning.

evidence.title: ReLU Strikes Back: Exploiting Activation Sparsity in Large Language Models (Mirzadeh et al., ICLR 2024)
evidence.quote: OPT-1.3B trained from scratch "on a hundred billion tokens of the RefinedWeb datasets with different activation functions, including ReLU, SiLU, and GELU"; "the performance of the models is very similar when using different activation functions"; no seeds or variance reported.
evidence.what_it_shows: Single-run 1.3B decoder parity of ReLU with GELU/SiLU on zero-shot benchmarks, plus ~90% activation sparsity for ReLU.

evidence.title: ReLU^2 Wins: Discovering Efficient Activation Functions for Sparse LLMs (Zhang et al., 2024)
evidence.quote: Four 1.3B LMs pretrained on 100B tokens: SwiGLU 50.53, ReGLU 50.36, ReLU^2 50.48, ReLU 48.85 average accuracy; "ReLU consistently underperforms" the GLU and squared variants; single run each.
evidence.what_it_shows: Plain ReLU trails gated/squared units by ~1.5 points at 1.3B, while squared ReLU (non-smooth) matches SwiGLU: the loss is about gating/squaring, not smoothness.

gap: A 12-seed matched-parameter ReLU-vs-GELU run at 10-60M would give the first sign-per-seed estimate at nano scale plus free activation-sparsity curves, but it would be replicating a parity already shown with 4-5 runs at 223M and single runs at 1.3B; the informative arm is ReLU^2 vs SwiGLU vs GELU, not ReLU vs GELU.
notes: Read this CONTESTED as 'controlled evidence is against the claim as worded'. Nothing controlled supports 'strictly worse than smooth activations': ReLU = GELU within run-to-run noise at 223M (two independent 4-5 run studies) and at 1.3B (single run). The 'for' side is (a) Hendrycks & Gimpel 2016's non-LM experiments that GPT-2/BERT inherited and (b) ReLU^2 Wins showing plain ReLU ~1.5 points below SwiGLU/ReLU^2 at 1.3B, which is a gating/squaring effect since non-smooth ReLU^2 matches SwiGLU. Our prior ('ReLU revival papers report parity') is confirmed but the parity evidence is stronger than we recorded: it has variance estimates at 223M. Recommend folding this claim into swiglu-better and adding a ReLU^2 arm rather than running it alone.

evidence.title: Rotary Embeddings: A Relative Revolution (EleutherAI blog, Biderman et al. 2021)
evidence.quote: 125M GPT-NeoX on OpenWebText2, 55k steps: Learned Absolute loss 2.809, T5 RPE 2.801, Rotary 2.759; 1.4B on the Pile, 8k steps: Learned 2.240, T5 2.223, Rotary 2.173; seeds not stated, hyperparameters copied from GPT-3 sizes without per-arm tuning.
evidence.what_it_shows: The most-cited in-distribution evidence: a ~0.05-0.07 nat RoPE win over learned at 125M and 1.4B, single run each, no sinusoidal arm.

evidence.title: Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases (Press et al., ICLR 2022)
evidence.quote: 247M WikiText-103 model evaluated at its training length L=1024: Sinusoidal 19.34, Rotary 19.33, T5 bias 18.80, ALiBi 18.66 perplexity; the sinusoidal baseline has std 0.24 across seeds (count not stated).
evidence.what_it_shows: In-distribution, RoPE is indistinguishable from sinusoidal at 247M; relative-bias methods beat both.

evidence.title: What Language Model to Train if You Have One Million GPU Hours? (Le Scao et al., 2022)
evidence.quote: 1.3B, 112B tokens, single run per arm, EAI-harness average: ALiBi 43.70, Learned 41.71, Rotary 41.46, None 41.23; ALiBi's lead held "even without taking into account their ability to extrapolate".
evidence.what_it_shows: The one contrary datapoint: learned >= rotary on downstream tasks at 1.3B, single run, noisy metric.

evidence.title: nanogpt-from-scratch paired-seed ablation study (unrefereed GitHub report)
evidence.quote: 51.2M params, 3 seeds, 524M tokens, T=1024: pos-rope -0.0886 +/- 0.0021 val loss vs learned absolute (seed noise floor 0.0043), all seeds agreed; pos-none +0.0928 +/- 0.0110.
evidence.what_it_shows: Nano-scale, matched-budget, 3-seed evidence that RoPE beats learned in-distribution by ~20x the noise floor; no sinusoidal arm.

gap: The sinusoidal arm is the missing one: every multi-run or nano-scale comparison pits RoPE against learned only, and the one study with sinusoidal (Press, 247M) finds a null, so a 12-seed learned vs sinusoidal vs RoPE panel at 10-60M would decide whether the claim is 'RoPE beats learned' or merely 'any fixed encoding beats a learned table at small data'.
notes: Our prior ('few seeds; most later evidence is extrapolation') is right. Vs LEARNED the sign is consistent across 51M (3 seeds), 125M, 1.4B in-distribution loss and only Scao's single-run downstream numbers disagree; expect the nano test to confirm this arm easily (delta ~0.09 nats at 51M/524M tokens). Vs SINUSOIDAL the claim is unsupported: Press finds 19.33 vs 19.34 at 247M, and Haviv 2022 finds sinusoidal beats learned (12.93 vs 13.05 at 1.3B), which together suggest the RoPE-over-learned gap may be mostly a learned-table penalty. Kazemnejad 2023 (3 seeds, 107M) reports all PEs at parity in-distribution on its synthetic tasks, and its 1.3B StarCoder run shows similar iid perplexity across variants. RoFormer's own MT/GLUE numbers (+0.2 BLEU, mixed GLUE) are not evidence for the LM claim.

evidence.title: Transformer Language Models without Positional Encodings Still Learn Positional Information (Haviv et al., EMNLP Findings 2022)
evidence.quote: 125M-1.3B on WikiText-103 and the Pile: WikiText NoPos 20.97 vs Learned 20.42 vs Sinusoidal 20.16 vs ALiBi 19.71; Pile 1.3B NoPos 13.10 vs Learned 13.05 vs Sinusoidal 12.93 vs ALiBi 12.51; "performance gaps narrow in larger models"; seed count not stated, and the paper itself notes concurrent work found up-to-0.9-perplexity seed gaps in this setting.
evidence.what_it_shows: NoPE is consistently but only slightly worse in-distribution, with the gap shrinking with scale; single-seed with an acknowledged seed noise comparable to the gap.

evidence.title: Length Generalization of Causal Transformers without Position Encoding (Wang et al., ACL Findings 2024)
evidence.quote: 1.1B NoPE and RoPE models trained on ~100B tokens at T=2048: within training length both average ~46.2 on commonsense benchmarks; NoPE "begins degrading significantly beyond 2.4K tokens", with the perplexity inflection tracking the attention-entropy inflection; a softmax temperature of 1.2/sqrt(d) extends it to 4.4K.
evidence.what_it_shows: Single-run 1.1B downstream parity in-distribution, and a concrete failure of the 'NoPE length-generalises' half beyond ~20% extra length.

evidence.title: Rope to Nope and Back Again: A New Hybrid Attention Strategy (Yang et al., Cohere 2025)
evidence.quote: 8B models from scratch (750B-token observation phase); "the NoPE variant lags behind" RoPE on standard benchmarks, confirming that NoPE models show "inferior performance in terms of perplexity and downstream task evaluations within the trained sequence length"; 16 seeds are used only for NIAH evaluation, not training.
evidence.what_it_shows: At 8B, pure NoPE loses in-distribution; the production answer became interleaved RoPE/NoPE (also Llama 4, SmolLM3), not NoPE.

evidence.title: nanogpt-from-scratch paired-seed ablation study (unrefereed GitHub report)
evidence.quote: 51.2M, 3 seeds, 524M tokens, T=1024: pos-none +0.0928 +/- 0.0110 vs learned and pos-rope -0.0886 +/- 0.0021, i.e. NoPE ~0.18 nats behind RoPE with every seed agreeing (noise floor 0.0043).
evidence.what_it_shows: At nano scale and short budget, NoPE is far from matching RoPE; the largest gap in the literature, consistent with Haviv's 'gap narrows with scale'.

gap: A 12-seed matched-budget none-vs-RoPE run at 10-60M would pin the in-distribution gap and its scaling with T where the 3-seed 51M result says it is largest (~0.18 nats); the length-generalisation probe is the more valuable half because Wang's 20% cliff and Kazemnejad's NoPE advantage have never been reconciled at one scale with seeds.
notes: The claim as worded ('NoPE matches RoPE') is scale-dependent and at nano scale almost certainly false: expect NoPE to lose in-distribution by an amount well outside a 12-seed band. Our prior is right that the small-model support (Kazemnejad 2023: 107M, 3 seeds, synthetic reasoning tasks, all PEs perfect in-distribution) is task-specific, and that later at-scale reports contest it. Note also Gu et al. 2025 found attention sinks emerge with NoPE just as with RoPE, so 'NoPE changes the sink story' is not a free extra result. The interesting nano question is not parity but the crossing: at what token budget/T does the NoPE penalty fall below the seed band.

evidence.title: When Attention Sink Emerges in Language Models: An Empirical View (Gu et al., ICLR 2025 spotlight)
evidence.quote: LLaMA-style models 60M-1B trained from scratch on 5B Pile tokens (default 60M: d768, 10 blocks, 8 heads, 20k steps); sinks appear "less obvious in LMs trained with small learning rates" and vanish below ~500M tokens; PE choice (NoPE/absolute/ALiBi/RoPE), pre/post-norm, FFN and head design have "negligible effects"; shifted-window attention with w=4-8 shows ~2-8% sink heads vs 18.18% at full context; sigmoid attention without normalisation: "LMs still have comparable validation loss but no attention sink" (60M 3.74 vs 3.73; 1B 3.10 vs 3.07); no seeds reported.
evidence.what_it_shows: The controlled from-scratch sweep: sinks are a softmax-normalisation artefact conditional on LR and data, not universal; removing them costs ~0.01-0.03 nats; small windows prevent emergence.

evidence.title: Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks (Xiao et al., ICLR 2024)
evidence.quote: Window attention that evicts the initial tokens collapses (Llama-2-13B perplexity 5.4 -> 5158 when the first four tokens are dropped); 160M models pretrained with a learnable sink token stream stably with that single token while vanilla models need several initial tokens; single runs.
evidence.what_it_shows: For softmax models with KV eviction, keeping the sink is necessary; a trained sink token suffices - the 'necessary for stable long context' half, in the eviction setting only.

evidence.title: Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity, Sparsity, and Attention-Sink-Free (Qiu et al., Qwen 2025)
evidence.quote: 1.7B dense and 15B-A2.5B MoE models on up to 3.5T tokens: an SDPA output gate cuts first-token attention share from 46.7% to 4.8%, "substantially enhanced training stability, mitigating loss spikes", tolerates LR 8e-3 where baselines diverge, lowers PPL by >0.2, and gains >10 RULER points at 128k; seeds not stated.
evidence.what_it_shows: Sink-free models are MORE stable and extrapolate better at scale: direct counter-evidence to 'necessary for stability', single-run.

evidence.title: Why do LLMs attend to the first token? (Barbero et al., 2025)
evidence.quote: Gemma 7B / Llama 3.1 8B-405B analysed, plus ~120M models trained from scratch on 5B tokens with context 128-4096: sink strength grows with model size and training context; removing <bos> at inference drops RULER to 0%; sinks argued to prevent over-mixing/rank collapse.
evidence.what_it_shows: The functional-role case for sinks, with a nano-scale from-scratch context-length sweep (single-seed) and an inference-time (not training-time) necessity test.

gap: Gu et al. already swept norm/PE/activation at 60M and found them irrelevant, so the proposed sweep is likely a null; what a 12-seed nano study would add is the emergence RATE per configuration (Gu is single-run) and the genuinely untested question of whether sink-free softmax runs (small LR, few tokens, or Softpick/sigmoid heads) fail on the window-attention lane, which no paper has measured.
notes: Both halves of the claim are wrong as absolutes. 'Emerge in every trained decoder': false, emergence needs softmax normalisation plus adequate LR and >~500M tokens, and sigmoid (Gu; Ramapuram et al. 2024 arXiv:2409.04431 matches softmax at 85M-7B), Softpick (arXiv:2504.20966: parity at 340M, but a 0.12-nat loss at 1.8B) and gated attention all train without sinks. 'Necessary for stable long-context attention': true only for softmax models with KV eviction (StreamingLLM), while sink-free gated models are more stable and extrapolate better. Theory (arXiv:2603.11487) proves sinks are forced in softmax attention for trigger-conditional 'no-op' tasks and removable with non-normalised attention, which reconciles the two sides. Correction to our prior: Gu's window-size dependence runs the opposite way to what we recorded (smaller windows PREVENT sinks), and Gu's models are 60M-1B with the default 60M, so the nano-scale emergence observation already exists in single-seed form. A 2026 survey (arXiv:2604.10098, 180+ papers) frames sinks as something to mitigate, not preserve.

evidence.title: SWAT: Sliding Window Attention Training for Efficient Large Language Models (Fu et al., 2025)
evidence.quote: 340M/15B-token and 760M/30B-token models from scratch; within training length (T=1024) sliding-window 3.02 vs full-attention 2.97 perplexity on OpenWebText, while at 16,384 tokens the window model holds 3.005 against full attention's 4.84; single run per arm.
evidence.what_it_shows: The only from-scratch matched-budget window-vs-full comparison at sub-1B scale: a ~1.7% in-distribution penalty for the window, single-seed, no training-curve or width analysis.

evidence.title: Gemma 3 Technical Report (Gemma Team, 2025)
evidence.quote: 2B text-only ablations: local:global ratios 1:1 to 7:1 - "The impact is minimal, even with 7-to-1 local to global"; window sizes 512-4096 at 1:1 and 1:3 - "the sliding window can be reduced significantly without impacting perplexity"; no long-context (RULER/NIAH) isolation of window size; single runs.
evidence.what_it_shows: At 2B with some global layers, perplexity is insensitive to window size; the loss the claim predicts does not show up in perplexity, only (untested here) on long-range evals.

evidence.title: Simple Local Attentions Remain Competitive for Long-Context Tasks (Xiong et al., NAACL 2022)
evidence.quote: RoBERTa-large variants pretrained "using the same long-doc corpus" (100k updates, 2^20 tokens per batch) then fine-tuned; "none of the tested efficient attentions can beat a simple local window attention"; MLM perplexity local window 3.47 vs blockwise 3.39 vs long-short 3.36; Hyperpartisan averaged over 4 seeds, other tasks single run.
evidence.what_it_shows: Controlled pretraining shows local attention is not worse than fancier sparse patterns on long-doc tasks; it does not include a same-length full-attention arm, so it is silent on the claim's comparison.

evidence.title: The Sparse Frontier: Sparse Attention Trade-offs in Transformer LLMs (Nawrot et al., 2025)
evidence.quote: "the largest-scale empirical analysis to date of training-free sparse attention, evaluating six methods across multiple model families and sizes, sequences up to 128K tokens, and sparsity levels up to 0.95" on nine tasks; local/window patterns degrade on long-range retrieval and reasoning tasks; "longer sequences tolerate higher sparsity".
evidence.what_it_shows: The long-range loss is measured post hoc on 7B-72B models, not trained in; it establishes the at-scale half of the claim only.

gap: No paper trains window vs full attention from scratch at matched budget with seeds and reports the training-time crossing or its dependence on width and T; the 'at every scale' clause and the early-lead/late-trail phenomenon seen in the transfer study are unreported, and even the in-distribution penalty (1.7% ppl at 340M, ~0 at 2B with global layers) has no variance estimate anywhere.
notes: Our prior stands: the literature measures long-range loss at scale on long-context benchmarks and never at nano scale as a function of training time. Two cautions for the design. First, in-distribution loss at T<=1k barely separates the arms (SWAT 1.7%, Gemma ~0), so the test needs a long-range probe (induction/copy at distance > window) or the crossing will sit inside the seed band; second, the recent post-training literature (Jolicoeur-Martineau 2026 arXiv:2608.28444: SWA with a 64-token window recovers ~99% of short-context performance on 1.3-70B models; SWAA arXiv:2512.10411) shows the window penalty is concentrated on retrieval-type tasks, so 'loses long-range dependencies' is really 'loses distant retrieval', and Gu et al. 2025 report that windows w<=8 also suppress sink formation, which couples this claim to sinks-necessary.

evidence.title: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints (Ainslie et al., EMNLP 2023)
evidence.quote: T5-XXL uptrained with 5% of pretraining compute: MHA-XXL 47.2, GQA-8-XXL 47.1, MQA-XXL 46.6 average; "we also do not compare our XXL GQA model to a comparative model trained from scratch, so we do not know the relative performance of uptraining vs training from scratch"; no seeds.
evidence.what_it_shows: The origin result is uptraining at one scale with no variance and, by its own admission, no from-scratch baseline; the 0.1-point gap is inside any plausible seed band.

evidence.title: Reducing Transformer Key-Value Cache Size with Cross-Layer Attention (Brandon et al., 2024)
evidence.quote: 1B models trained from scratch on 30B SlimPajama tokens with identical data order and "approximately the same number of FLOPs": validation perplexity MHA 13.15, GQA-4 13.36, MQA 13.54; single run per configuration, KV projections not compensated by extra width.
evidence.what_it_shows: From scratch at 1B, GQA-4 costs ~1.6% perplexity and MQA ~3% against MHA: measurable, single-seed, unmatched parameters.

evidence.title: Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need (Shazeer 2019)
evidence.quote: WMT14 En-De, all variants held at 211M parameters by widening d_ff from 4096 to 5440 for multi-query; dev perplexity multi-head 1.424 vs multi-query 1.439, dev BLEU 26.7 vs 26.5, "minor quality degradation"; single run.
evidence.what_it_shows: The only parameter-matched MQA-vs-MHA design in the lineage: still a small measurable loss, MT not LM, single seed.

evidence.title: nanogpt-from-scratch paired-seed ablation study (unrefereed GitHub report)
evidence.quote: 51.2M, 3 seeds, 524M tokens: gqa-2 (8 -> 2 KV heads) +0.0311 +/- 0.0012 val loss, every seed agreed, classed "Worse"; width was not adjusted to compensate for the KV-head reduction.
evidence.what_it_shows: At nano scale with seeds, a 4x KV reduction costs ~7x the noise floor in loss when parameters are not re-spent.

gap: A 12-seed matched-parameter (heads/d_ff adjusted) MHA vs GQA vs MQA run at 10-60M would be the first parameter-matched multi-seed comparison for a language model at any scale: Shazeer's matched design is MT and single-run, Brandon's and the 51M study are unmatched, and Ainslie's is uptraining.
notes: Read TESTED-WEAK as 'tested weakly, and the weak evidence runs AGAINST the claim as worded'. Every from-scratch comparison found shows a small, consistent loss for fewer KV heads (Shazeer 2019; Brandon 2024; DeepSeek-V2 arXiv:2405.04434 Appendix D at ~7B: GQA/MQA "performance does not match MHA"; the 51M 3-seed study), and Chen et al. 2025 (arXiv:2503.09579, 3M-1.2B from scratch, no seeds) treat the KV-head count as a real term in loss that must be bought back with model size. 'Loses nothing measurable' is therefore false at unmatched parameters and untested at matched parameters for LMs; the defensible claim is 'costs less than 2% perplexity, recoverable by re-spending the parameters', which is what practitioners actually rely on. Our prior ('uptrained, few seeds; from-scratch small-scale rarely reported') is right except that there is now a 3-seed nano datapoint and it shows a clear loss.

evidence.title: Small-scale proxies for large-scale Transformer training instabilities (Wortsman et al.)
evidence.quote: By measuring the relationship between learning rate and loss across scales, we show that these instabilities also appear in small models when training at high learning rates, and that mitigations previously employed at large scales are equally effective in this regime. ... Without qk-layernorm, the learning rate at which models diverge becomes smaller with increasing model size. By contrast, models with qk-layernorm exhibit considerably lower LR sensitivity and train to low loss at high learning rates.
evidence.what_it_shows: The alternative (no qk-layernorm) is actually run, at 10M to 4.8B parameters, across LR sweeps, matched steps. Single seed throughout; no seed count reported. The stability half of the claim is tested; the 'free in quality' half is only visual (curves overlap at low LR in Fig. 1) and never quantified at the per-arm optimal LR.

evidence.title: Methods of improving LLM training stability (Rybakov et al.)
evidence.quote: Reproducing training instabilities can be costly, so we use a small language model with 830M parameters and experiment with higher learning rates to force models to diverge. ... we observe significant perplexity improvements for all three methods in comparison to the baseline model.
evidence.what_it_shows: 830M model, QK-layernorm and variants vs baseline; perplexity gains reported but single seed and the gain is delivered through a higher LR ceiling rather than at a fixed LR.

evidence.title: 2 OLMo 2 Furious (OLMo Team)
evidence.quote: Applying layer norm after the attention and feedforward layers along with a QK-norm improves stability compared to a more standard pre-attention layer norm, reducing the spike score of the gradients from 0.108 to 0.069 when applied together. In isolation, neither of these changes yield good results, but together they improve both the growth and the spikiness of the L2 norm of the gradient.
evidence.what_it_shows: Large-scale stability ablation, one run per arm; QK-norm is confounded with the post-norm reordering (they report it does not help in isolation).

evidence.title: Controlling changes to attention logits (Anson et al.)
evidence.quote: Applying normalization to queries and keys, known as 'QK norm', fixes stability issues in practice, but is not always applicable. For example, QK norm is not compatible with Multi Latent Attention (MLA).
evidence.what_it_shows: ~1B Qwen3-style model, 5k steps, single seed; QK norm is the strong baseline and the proposed alternative is slightly worse in MHA, indirect evidence that QK norm costs nothing at that scale but no seeds and no matched-budget quality measurement.

gap: No study runs with/without QK-norm at the per-arm optimal LR with seeds; a 12-seed matched-budget nano test would establish whether 'free in quality' holds at the tuned LR (not just that it raises the LR ceiling) and whether attention-logit growth is even present at 10M to 60M parameters.
notes: Prior is right that Wortsman is the small-scale proxy, but it is single-seed and the quality claim is visual. Every positive result conflates two effects: LR-ceiling extension and per-LR quality. The nano test must sweep LR per arm or it will simply re-measure the LR ceiling. Two caveats for the design: QK-norm is incompatible with MLA, and a widely circulated (non-peer-reviewed) argument says it harms long-context retrieval by stripping query magnitude; neither is tested at nano scale.

evidence.title: An Empirical Study of muP Learning Rate Transfer (Lingle)
evidence.quote: Studying over a dozen ablations with up to 1.2B parameters and 33B tokens and a large-scale experiment with up to 10B parameters and 190B tokens, we observe a positive answer for most settings. ... the usual 1/sqrt(D) attention scale appears quite suboptimal, yielding worse performance ... The same seed is used for all experiments. ... For STP Attention Scale with fixed D in {32,128}, float32 precision resolves the lack of transfer.
evidence.what_it_shows: The only head-to-head 1/sqrt(D) vs 1/D transformer comparison found: widths 128/512/2048, head dim fixed at 128, single seed in bf16; 1/D gives lower loss and transfers, 1/sqrt(D) is worse and its transfer failure was partly a bf16 artefact (resolved in fp32 with 3 seeds). Because head dim is fixed, this is a constant-factor temperature test, not a width-scaling test.

evidence.title: Tensor Programs V: Tuning Large Neural Networks via Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer (Yang et al.)
evidence.quote: by transferring from 40M parameters, we outperform published numbers of the 6.7B GPT-3 model, with tuning cost only 7% of total pretraining cost.
evidence.what_it_shows: Introduces the 1/d_head attention scale with a base-d compatibility multiplier alpha_attn; 1/sqrt(d) vs 1/d is never run head-to-head at matched budget with seeds; it is a component of the parameterization, adopted not tested.

evidence.title: Scaling Exponents Across Parameterizations and Optimizers (Everett et al.)
evidence.quote: Our extensive empirical investigation includes tens of thousands of models trained with all combinations of three optimizers, four parameterizations, several alignment assumptions, more than a dozen learning rates, and fourteen model sizes up to 26.8B parameters.
evidence.what_it_shows: Attention scale is set per parameterization (sqrt(h) for SP/NTK, h for muP/mean-field) as an assumption, not ablated; no seeds reported.

evidence.title: Learning to Focus: Focal Attention for Selective and Scalable Transformers
evidence.quote: Learnable temperature rescales attention logits before softmax normalization and allows each layer to adapt the sharpness of its attention distribution.
evidence.what_it_shows: A proposal paper: learned temperature is presented as a method, not as a controlled, seeded, matched-budget alternative to 1/sqrt(d); no learned-temperature pretraining test with seeds was found in any vocabulary.

gap: A 12-seed nano sweep of 1/sqrt(d) vs 1/d vs learned temperature at per-arm optimal LR would be the first seeded test of the Vaswani constant; nothing in the literature separates 'the temperature constant is wrong' from 'the width exponent is wrong'.
notes: The claim as written conflates width with head dimension: both Vaswani's 1/sqrt(d_k) and muP's 1/d are functions of d_head, and in practice d_head is held fixed (64 or 128) while width grows, so both rules are constants and 'at every width' is vacuous unless the test scales d_head with width. Redesign: either vary d_head, or treat this as a temperature-constant test (1/sqrt(d) vs 1/d differs by ~8x to 11x at d_head 64 to 128). Prior is roughly right: an init-variance argument plus one single-seed empirical test (Lingle) showing 1/d better; muP's 1/d rule is adopted, not tested, in Everett and Yang.

evidence.title: Fantastic Pretraining Optimizers and Where to Find Them (Wen et al.)
evidence.quote: Matrix-based optimizers all deliver approximately a 1.3x speedup over AdamW [for models under 520M] ... speedup decays ... to only 1.1x for 1.2B parameter models ... in each iteration, we hold all but one hyperparameter fixed at the current best values, then search the whole grid for that parameter, and accept the new value if the validation loss improves by more than Delta_1 = 3e-3.
evidence.what_it_shows: 130M to 1.2B Llama-style models, per-optimizer coordinate-descent tuning, matched tokens across 1x to 8x Chinchilla; Muon beats a well-tuned AdamW by ~1.3x at nano-to-small scale, shrinking with size. No seeds or variance reported; ranking decisions rest on 3e-3 loss deltas.

evidence.title: Benchmarking Optimizers for Large Language Model Pretraining (Semenov et al.)
evidence.quote: We run each method 5 times with different seeds, compute the standard deviation, and report the mean wall-clock time per 100 iterations. ... we also try different gradient clipping levels, warmup steps, weight decay values, weights initialization, and learning rate schedulers. ... across model sizes used in our benchmarking of dense LLMs, we observe a major improvement of D-Muon over Muon.
evidence.what_it_shows: Independent benchmark, 124M to 720M, 11 optimizers, wall-clock measured with 5 seeds but loss rankings single-seed; plain Muon degrades with scale and needs decoupled weight decay (D-Muon); AdEMAMix ranked best; alternatives beat tuned AdamW by ~1.1x to 1.4x.

evidence.title: No Train No Gain: Revisiting Efficient Training Algorithms For Transformer-Based Language Models (Kaddour et al.)
evidence.quote: When pre-training BERT and T5 with a fixed computation budget using such methods, we find that their training, validation, and downstream gains vanish compared to a baseline with a fully-decayed learning rate.
evidence.what_it_shows: The sceptical side, at matched wall-clock (reference system time): Lion and Sophia do not beat AdamW. Muon was not tested; encoder/enc-dec models.

evidence.title: Practical Efficiency of Muon for Pretraining (Essential AI)
evidence.quote: We demonstrate that Muon, the simplest instantiation of a second-order optimizer, explicitly expands the Pareto frontier over AdamW on the compute-time tradeoff. ... We validate our findings through extensive experiments with model sizes up to four billion parameters.
evidence.what_it_shows: 100M to 4B, muP-tuned both sides; Muon needs 10 to 15 percent fewer tokens and retains efficiency past the critical batch size; single seed.

gap: No optimizer benchmark reports seeds at the ~3e-3 loss deltas that decide rankings; a 12-seed nano test at matched tokens AND matched wall-clock with per-optimizer LR sweeps would show whether the ~1.3x Muon advantage at 100M exceeds seed noise and survives wall-clock accounting at 10M to 60M.
notes: The prior is backwards: it is the AdamW baseline that was under-tuned in most optimizer papers (a 2x speedup is available by tuning AdamW's LR alone), and once tuned, Muon still wins at <=500M by ~1.3x in two independent benchmarks, but the ~2x Moonshot claim does not survive and the advantage shrinks toward 1.0x to 1.1x by 1.2B. Expect Muon to beat AdamW at nano scale at matched tokens; the open questions are seed significance, wall-clock, and whether plain Muon (vs D-Muon) is stable in the muP-free regime. Kaddour's fixed-budget null did not include Muon.

evidence.title: On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture (Xiong et al.)
evidence.quote: We show in our experiments that Pre-LN Transformers without the warm-up stage can reach comparable results with baselines while requiring significantly less training time and hyper-parameter tuning on a wide range of applications.
evidence.what_it_shows: Pre-LN trains without warmup on NMT and BERT; the alternative is actually run, but single runs, no seeds, LR not swept per arm.

evidence.title: Analyzing & Reducing the Need for Learning Rate Warmup in GPT Training (Kosson et al.)
evidence.quote: Focusing on small-scale GPT training with AdamW/Lion ... we find that warmup helps counteract large angular updates as well as a limited critical batch size early in training. ... Not using warmup results in faster initial progress for a given learning rate, but eventually falls behind leaving a permanent gap.
evidence.what_it_shows: 124M GPT-2, OpenWebText, pre-norm, batch 480: no divergence without warmup but a lasting loss gap at fixed LR; seeds not reported; the gap can be removed by normalising update size in the optimizer.

evidence.title: Why Warmup the Learning Rate? Underlying Mechanisms and Improvements (Kalra & Barkeshli, NeurIPS 2024)
evidence.quote: The overwhelming benefit of warmup arises from allowing the network to tolerate larger target learning rates by forcing the network to more well-conditioned areas of the loss landscape. ... test accuracy primarily depends on the target learning rate and nominally on the warmup duration.
evidence.what_it_shows: ~2M-parameter pre-LN transformers on WikiText-2 plus ResNets/MLPs; warmup's effect is through the LR ceiling; seeds not stated; scale is below the nano range.

evidence.title: Resolving Discrepancies in Compute-Optimal Scaling of Language Models (Porian et al.)
evidence.quote: The steps taken to settle the discrepancy (namely shortening warmup and scaling learning rate and batch size) significantly decrease loss at smaller scales, but only marginally improve it at larger scales.
evidence.what_it_shows: Long (Kaplan-style) warmup hurts small models; supports shorter-not-zero warmup; single seed.

gap: No seeded study separates 'stability' (divergence count) from 'final loss at per-arm optimal LR'; a 12-seed nano test with LR swept per warmup arm would say whether warmup-0 loses anything once the LR is retuned, and how often it diverges at 10M to 60M.
notes: Prior is right. The strict claim ('necessary for stability') is false for pre-norm per Xiong and Kosson (no divergence); the softer claim ('warmup lowers final loss at a fixed LR') holds single-seed at 124M. The brief's test as written (same LR across arms) will reproduce Kosson's permanent gap and be confounded by LR tolerance; add a per-arm LR sweep or it measures the LR ceiling, not warmup. Warmup's effect also depends on batch size (Kosson ties it to early critical batch size), so fix batch across arms.

evidence.title: Scaling Laws and Compute-Optimal Training Beyond Fixed Training Durations (Hägele et al.)
evidence.quote: we observe an almost perfect match between the performance of the best cosine and cooldown schedule even for different training durations, all while exhibiting slightly less sensitivity to variations in the LR.
evidence.what_it_shows: 33M to 360M (plus 1B and 8B checks), cosine vs constant-plus-cooldown (~20 percent, 1-sqrt shape), LR swept for both; WSD matches cosine. Seeds not reported.

evidence.title: Straight to Zero: Why Linearly Decaying the Learning Rate to Zero Works Best for LLMs (Bergsma et al., ICLR 2025)
evidence.quote: Training runs use the same random seed, so all decay functions (Linear, Cosine, etc.) and decay ratios (Constant, 10x, D2Z) have identical warmups, but note results are very consistent across seeds at this scale (appendix Figure 24). ... For 610M-parameter muP models trained to compute-optimal 20 TPP, the optimal Linear-D2Z setting achieves 0.77% lower loss than the optimal Linear-10x setting. ... Linear-D2Z slightly outperforms Cosine-D2Z in all cases.
evidence.what_it_shows: 111M to 1.7B, LR swept per schedule, matched tokens: decay-to-zero beats decay-to-10 percent consistently; linear beats cosine slightly; D2Z beats the best WSD by ~0.84 percent at 80 TPP. Single seed with an appendix seed-consistency check.

evidence.title: Understanding Warmup-Stable-Decay Learning Rates: A River Valley Loss Landscape Perspective (Wen et al.)
evidence.quote: Understanding Warmup-Stable-Decay Learning Rates: A River Valley Loss Landscape Perspective
evidence.what_it_shows: Mechanistic account of why a late decay recovers the cosine loss; used here only as corroboration that WSD-vs-cosine equivalence is theory-backed, not as a seeded test (quote is the title; the abstract page was not fetched).

gap: None of these report seed counts; a 12-seed test at 10M to 60M would show whether the 0.5 to 1 percent schedule effects (D2Z vs 10 percent floor; WSD vs cosine) exceed seed noise at nano scale, where noise is larger than at 600M.
notes: Prior is wrong in one part: 'cosine to ~10 percent' is not the best schedule. With per-arm LR sweeps, decay to zero (linear or cosine) is consistently better by ~0.5 to 1 percent loss (Bergsma), and WSD matching cosine (Hägele) is supported but with unreported seeds. Add a decay-to-zero arm and sweep LR per schedule (the optimal peak LR differs by schedule; Bergsma shows D2Z tolerates a higher peak). The third evidence entry is weak by construction and should be replaced if a seeded WSD-vs-cosine study surfaces.

evidence.title: Why Do We Need Weight Decay in Modern Deep Learning? (Andriushchenko et al., NeurIPS 2024)
evidence.quote: For underparameterized large language models trained with nearly online SGD, weight decay balances the bias-variance tradeoff in stochastic optimization leading to lower training loss. ... a 124M parameter model (known as GPT-2-Small) ... on OpenWebText ... 50 000 iterations with a batch size of 256 ... 3 different random seeds ... the final training loss is smaller for lambda equal to 0.1 and 0.3 compared to 0.
evidence.what_it_shows: Matched iterations, 3 seeds, wd 0 vs 0.1 vs 0.3 at 124M: training loss is lower with wd, but the benefit appears only after the 10x cosine decay and is reproduced by matching the effective-LR trajectory, i.e. it is an LR-schedule effect.

evidence.title: Training Optimal Large Diffusion Language Models (Quokka; Ni et al.)
evidence.quote: neither AR nor DLM benefits from weight decay in this regime; in fact, removing weight decay leads to faster convergence. ... removing weight decay severely degrades AR models' validation loss and benchmark performance [96 epochs on 1B unique tokens].
evidence.what_it_shows: 1B autoregressive model, 96B tokens single-epoch: wd 0 converged faster; the benefit of wd only appears under heavy data repetition. Single seed, LR presumably not re-tuned per arm; the one controlled contradiction at scale.

evidence.title: Power Lines: Scaling Laws for Weight Decay and Batch Size in LLM Pre-training (Bergsma et al., NeurIPS 2025)
evidence.quote: Recent work suggests the AdamW timescale, tau = B/(eta lambda D), should remain constant across training settings, and we verify the implication that optimal lambda scales linearly with B, for a fixed N and D. However, as N and D scale, we show optimal tau obeys a precise power law in the tokens-per-parameter ratio, D/N.
evidence.what_it_shows: Optimal wd is strictly positive but depends on B, eta, D and N; 0.1 is not a universal constant, and a short nano run at small batch can have an optimal lambda far from 0.1. Single seed, muP models.

gap: A 12-seed nano test with wd swept (0, 0.01, 0.1, 0.3) and LR swept per arm, recording train and validation loss separately, would tell whether the training-loss benefit at 10M to 60M is a fixed-LR artefact of the effective-LR schedule or a genuine optimisation gain.
notes: Prior is mostly right (3 seeds at 124M support lower training loss with wd), but two corrections: (1) the mechanism means a wd-0 arm at the same LR is not a fair alternative, since wd acts as an LR-schedule modifier, so LR must be swept per arm; (2) '0.1' is not a magic constant (Bergsma; Semenov also found 0.5 better on short runs and 0.1 on long ones). Quokka's 1B single-epoch result is the one controlled contradiction, but single seed and no LR re-tune. The claim's 'not just generalisation' framing is well supported: nobody finds wd acting as a classical regulariser in single-epoch LM pretraining.

evidence.title: Tensor Programs V: Tuning Large Neural Networks via Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer (Yang et al.)
evidence.quote: We show that, in the recently discovered Maximal Update Parametrization (muP), many optimal HPs remain stable even as model size changes. ... by transferring pretraining HPs from a model of 13M parameters, we outperform published numbers of BERT-large (350M parameters) ... by transferring from 40M parameters, we outperform published numbers of the 6.7B GPT-3 model.
evidence.what_it_shows: muP LR transfer demonstrated on transformers at two scales; the SP-optimum-falls-with-width claim is shown in sweep figures, not with seeds; no seed counts reported.

evidence.title: An Empirical Study of muP Learning Rate Transfer (Lingle)
evidence.quote: Studying over a dozen ablations with up to 1.2B parameters and 33B tokens and a large-scale experiment with up to 10B parameters and 190B tokens, we observe a positive answer for most settings, and discuss improvements otherwise. ... for all model sizes, the optimal loss in the sweep is higher [for standard parameterization] than the optimal loss for the baseline muP models. ... The same seed is used for all experiments.
evidence.what_it_shows: Independent replication: muP LR transfer holds for most settings up to 10B; failures tied to trainable gains, bf16 attention scale and unembedding init; single seed.

evidence.title: Scaling Exponents Across Parameterizations and Optimizers (Everett et al.)
evidence.quote: Our results show that all parameterizations, not just maximal update parameterization (muP), can achieve hyperparameter transfer; moreover, our novel per-layer learning rate prescription for standard parameterization outperforms muP.
evidence.what_it_shows: 14 sizes up to 26.8B, tens of thousands of runs: SP with per-layer LR transfers too and beats muP; the global-LR SP optimum drifts with width but not as the naive 1/width; no seeds reported.

evidence.title: On the Surprising Effectiveness of Large Learning Rates under Standard Width Scaling (Haas et al., NeurIPS 2025)
evidence.quote: In practice, however, optimal learning rates decay slower than theoretically predicted and networks exhibit both stable training and non-trivial feature learning, even at very large widths. ... width-scaling considerations are surprisingly useful for predicting empirically maximal stable learning rate exponents which provide useful guidance on optimal learning rate exponents.
evidence.what_it_shows: Pythia-GPT up to width 4096 / 1.4B under SP: the optimal LR falls with width but slower than 1/width (controlled-divergence regime under CE loss); seeds not stated.

gap: Nothing measures seed noise of lr*(width) at nano scale; a 12-seed matched-token sweep would show whether the brief's non-monotone lr* (2.5e-4, 5e-4, 1.25e-4) is noise on a broad optimum (Step Law reports a broad convex optimum) or a real small-width effect, and whether the SP exponent at 10M to 60M is nearer -1 or -0.5.
notes: Prior needs correction in two directions. (1) '1/width under SP' is the Adam-SP theoretical prediction, but Everett and Haas both find empirically slower decay, and Everett finds SP transfers fine with per-layer LR, so the SP half of the claim is contested by the two largest sweeps in the literature. (2) The 'muP makes it constant' half is supported by three independent single-seed studies (Yang, Lingle, Everett) and would be TESTED-WEAK on its own. The nano non-monotone observation is most likely within seed noise on a broad optimum; also note that widths 256 to 1024 with fixed d_head may sit below the regime where width exponents are measurable, and the sweep grid (factor-2 steps) is coarser than the effect.

evidence.title: Gradient Shaping Beyond Clipping: A Functional Perspective on Update Magnitude Control
evidence.quote: language modeling with a 12-layer GPT-style decoder on WikiText-103 (truncated subset) ... All models are trained with batch size 128, initial learning rate 0.001 (for Adam), and a cosine decay schedule ... repeat experiments with 3 different seeds to report average and variance. [Table 1 WikiText-103 perplexity: Baseline 41.2 +/- 1.3; Fixed Clipping 35.5 +/- 1.0]
evidence.what_it_shows: The only seeded no-clip vs fixed-clip comparison found in a transformer LM: 3 seeds, ~100M-class GPT, matched steps. But a single LR shared across arms, so the no-clip arm is not LR-retuned, and a 14 percent perplexity gap from clipping alone is implausibly large, pointing to an LR confound.

evidence.title: ZClip: Adaptive Spike Mitigation for LLM Pre-Training
evidence.quote: a 1B (16 layers) LLaMA model [trained on] 50 billion tokens ... 1) training without clipping, 2) clipping with fixed threshold 1.0, and 3) ZClip ... [at LR 3.0e-3] ZClip [final loss] 2.14 compared to fixed-threshold's 5.14.
evidence.what_it_shows: The alternative (no clipping) and clip 1.0 are both run at 1B across LRs: clip 1.0 does not by itself prevent divergence at high LR, and no-clip diverges earlier; the effect is conditional on LR; seeds not specified.

evidence.title: Why Gradient Clipping Accelerates Training: A Theoretical Justification for Adaptivity (Zhang et al., ICLR 2020)
evidence.quote: experiments in computer vision and language modeling demonstrate that clipping accelerates training error convergence and allows the training trajectory to cross non-smooth regions of the loss landscape.
evidence.what_it_shows: Relaxed-smoothness theory plus LSTM/PTB experiments; not a transformer, not matched-budget with seeds; this is the paper usually cited for the claim.

evidence.title: Writing an LLM from scratch, part 32b: Interventions: gradient clipping (Giles Thomas blog)
evidence.quote: three places where the loss suddenly spiked up, at around global steps 4,200, 13,000, and 23,000 [unclipped] ... only two small loss spikes [clipped at 3.5] ... test set loss of 3.678 compared to the baseline's 3.692, a reduction of 0.014, or about 0.3%.
evidence.what_it_shows: 163M GPT-2 on 3.26B FineWeb tokens, single run each: spikes exist without clipping at this scale and the final-loss difference (0.3 percent) is inside typical seed noise. Hobby-scale, single seed, threshold 3.5 not 1.0.

gap: No study at any scale runs clip 1.0 vs none vs a loose threshold with LR swept per arm and seeds, recording spike counts; the 12-seed nano test would be the first, and would also establish whether spikes occur at all at 10M to 60M with pre-norm AdamW.
notes: Prior ('no controlled small-scale study in wide circulation') is nearly right: the one seeded comparison is buried in Table 1 of a methods paper and is LR-confounded; Semenov tuned the clip threshold but never ablated it; AdaGC compares adaptive vs global clipping at 7B/13B, never vs none. As with QK-norm and warmup, clipping's value at nano scale may be entirely an LR-ceiling effect, so sweep LR per arm. A further confound: late-training gradient-norm growth is argued to be a weight-decay/normalisation artefact (Defazio et al. 2025, 'Why gradients rapidly increase near the end of training'), so clipping frequency late in the run is not the same phenomenon as early spikes; log both.

evidence.title: How Does Critical Batch Size Scale in Pre-training? (Zhang et al., ICLR 2025)
evidence.quote: we propose a measure of CBS and pre-train a series of auto-regressive language models, ranging from 85 million to 1.2 billion parameters, on the C4 dataset. Through extensive hyper-parameter sweeps and careful control of factors such as batch size, momentum, and learning rate along with its scheduling, we systematically investigate the impact of scale on CBS. ... our results demonstrate that CBS scales primarily with data size rather than model size.
evidence.what_it_shows: CBS measured directly (20 percent step inflation vs linear scaling) with batch 64 to 16k sequences, matched tokens; 85M model CBS ~ 2^9.5 sequences; a constant LR across batch sizes was optimal. Seeds not reported.

evidence.title: Critical Batch Size Revisited: A Simple Empirical Approach to Large-Batch Language Model Training (Merrill et al., NeurIPS 2025)
evidence.quote: strong assumptions are required to justify gradient noise as a proxy for the CBS, which makes it unclear whether their approach should be trusted in practice. ... For both OLMo 1B and 7B models, the gradient noise scale underestimates the CBS by several orders of magnitude.
evidence.what_it_shows: McCandlish's gradient-noise-scale proxy fails at 1B and 7B; CBS must be measured directly by branching runs; single runs per branch.

evidence.title: Power Lines: Scaling Laws for Weight Decay and Batch Size in LLM Pre-training (Bergsma et al., NeurIPS 2025)
evidence.quote: We also study scaling laws for optimal batch size B_opt (the B enabling lowest loss at a given N,D) and critical batch size B_crit (the B beyond which further data parallelism becomes ineffective). In contrast to prior work, we find both B_opt and B_crit scale as power laws in D, independent of model size, N.
evidence.what_it_shows: Independent confirmation that CBS grows with data (hence loss), not model size; separates B_opt from B_crit; single seed, muP.

evidence.title: Small Batch Size Training for Language Models: When Vanilla SGD Works, and Why Gradient Accumulation Is Wasteful (Marek et al.)
evidence.quote: we revisit small batch sizes all the way down to batch size one, and we propose a rule for scaling Adam hyperparameters to small batch sizes. ... We find that small batch sizes (1) train stably, (2) are consistently more robust to hyperparameter choices, (3) achieve equal or better per-FLOP performance than larger batch sizes.
evidence.what_it_shows: 19M, 30M, 124M, 1.3B models, batch 1 to 4096, beta_2 half-life held fixed in tokens: small batches are not wasteful per FLOP, only per step; no error bars.

gap: A 12-seed matched-token batch sweep at 10M would give the first seeded CBS estimate at nano scale and test whether the 20 percent step-inflation definition is resolvable above seed noise there; nothing in the literature goes below ~19M or reports seeds.
notes: Prior needs three fixes. (1) McCandlish's claim is that small batches are MORE sample-efficient and large batches waste compute above the CBS; 'small-batch training is wasteful' is a misreading (true only in steps/wall-clock), and Marek confirms per-FLOP parity down to batch 1. (2) The gradient-noise-scale proxy half of McCandlish is refuted at 1B/7B (Merrill). (3) CBS depends on data/loss, not model size (Zhang, Bergsma), so at 10M with few tokens the CBS will be small (hundreds of sequences). Design warnings: the brief's 'lr scaled' rule is itself contested (Zhang found a constant LR optimal across batch sizes for Adam), and beta_2 must be retuned at small batch (Porian; Marek) or small-batch arms will look artificially bad.

evidence.title: The Impact of Depth and Width on Transformer Language Model Generalization (Petty, van Steenkiste, Dasgupta, Sha, Garrette, Linzen)
evidence.quote: we construct three classes of models which trade off depth for width such that the total number of parameters is kept constant (41M, 134M and 374M parameters) ... within each family, deeper models show better language modeling performance, but returns are similarly diminishing. [Body: 'Mean over 5 runs shown with error bars'; C4, 1M steps ~131B tokens; 41M family spans 1-7 layers; performance 'begins to degrade when models become too narrow', once d_ff < d_model.]
evidence.what_it_shows: The only parameter-matched depth-width sweep with seeds at nano scale (41M, 5 runs): depth helps with rapidly diminishing returns and an interior optimum once the FFN gets narrower than d_model. Directly covers the proposed design except that the 41M family only reaches 7 layers.

evidence.title: The Depth Delusion: Why Transformers Should Be Wider, Not Deeper (Fahim, Karim)
evidence.quote: validated across 30 transformer architectures spanning 17M to 7B parameters ... Beyond a critical depth threshold D_crit ~ W^0.44 ... adding layers increases loss despite adding parameters. [Body: 'we fix the random seed (S=42) for weight initialization and data shuffling across all experiments'; at W=512, 16L (102M) loss 3.435 beats 24L (127M) 3.468 and 32L (153M) 3.441.]
evidence.what_it_shows: Single-seed but wide grid (2-80 layers, 256-6144 width): confirms an interior optimum and locates it at roughly 12-16 layers for d_model=512, i.e. the monotone form of the claim is false and the optimum sits inside the nano range.

evidence.title: MobileLLM: Optimizing Sub-billion Parameter Language Models for On-Device Use Cases (Liu et al.)
evidence.quote: we trained 19 models, including 9 models with ~125M parameters and 10 models with ~350M parameters ... layers from 4 to 62 ... Deeper and thinner models outperform their shallower and wider counterparts; models with 30 or even 42 layers perform significantly better than those with 12 layers. [No seeds or variance reported.]
evidence.what_it_shows: Single-run, downstream-accuracy evidence that at 125M depth 30-42 beats 12; the most-cited practitioner source for 'deep and thin'. Its optimum (30-42 layers at d~512) is inconsistent with Depth Delusion's ~15, which is exactly the kind of disagreement seeds would resolve.

evidence.title: Limits to Depth Efficiencies of Self-Attention (Levine, Wies, Sharir, Bata, Shashua)
evidence.quote: we pinpoint a depth threshold that is logarithmic in the network width: for networks of depth below the threshold, we establish a double-exponential depth-efficiency ... for depths over the threshold, depth-inefficiency kicks in ... we further demonstrate the two depth-(in)efficiency regimes experimentally for common network depths of 6, 12, and 24.
evidence.what_it_shows: Theory plus ablations predicting an optimal depth ~ log(width); the origin of the 'optimum per width' framing. Kaplan et al. 2020's 'shape matters little' is the weak-effect version over the same interior region.

gap: No seeded, matched-token grid at 10-60M crosses the depth optimum: Petty's 41M family stops at 7 layers (5 runs) and the only sweep that crosses D_crit at that width is single-seed, so a 12-seed layers x d grid would give the first variance-backed location and width of the nano-scale optimum (and adjudicate MobileLLM's 30-42 vs Depth Delusion's ~15).
notes: Our prior is right but the claim is mis-stated: every controlled source (Petty with 5 seeds, Depth Delusion, MobileLLM, Levine, Kaplan) finds an interior optimum, not 'deeper wins'. Petty already answers the proposed test at 41M for 1-7 layers, so the study's value is the deep side of the optimum and the seed variance, not the sign. Depth Delusion is a 2026 preprint with one seed and error bars from the last 10% of training tokens; treat its exponents as provisional.

evidence.title: PaLM: Scaling Language Modeling with Pathways (Chowdhery et al.)
evidence.quote: Ablation experiments showed a small quality degradation at 8B scale but no quality degradation at 62B scale, so we extrapolated that the effect of parallel layers should be quality neutral at the 540B scale.
evidence.what_it_shows: The canonical test: a single-run ablation at 8B and 62B, sequential actually run. It records a small cost at the smaller scale, which is the opposite of 'costs nothing' below 8B.

evidence.title: The Falcon Series of Open Language Models (Almazrouei et al.)
evidence.quote: We found no measurable degradation in zero-shot performance or perplexity, in line with Chowdhery et al. (2022), and adopt this practice. [Ablation at 1B parameters, 30B tokens; seeds not stated.]
evidence.what_it_shows: The only published sub-8B ablation: 1B / 30B tokens, single run, null result on zero-shot and Pile perplexity. No variance estimate, so 'no measurable' is bounded by one run's noise.

evidence.title: Pythia: A Suite for Analyzing Large Language Models Across Training and Scaling (Biderman et al.)
evidence.quote: we use parallel attention and feedforward ... even though it is generally not recommended for models with less than 6B parameters ... we found that despite making choices we expected to hurt performance at smaller scales, our models perform the same as equi-parameter OPT models.
evidence.what_it_shows: Adoption, not a test: parallel used at 70M-12B and compared to a different family (OPT) trained on different data. Widely cited as evidence that parallel is free at small scale; it is not a controlled comparison.

evidence.title: GPT-NeoX-20B: An Open-Source Autoregressive Language Model (Black et al.)
evidence.quote: this led to a 15% throughput increase while having comparable loss curves with running them in series during early training. [Describes the mesh-transformer-jax / GPT-J origin.]
evidence.what_it_shows: The origin claim rests on eyeballed early-training loss curves in one run; no numbers, no seeds, no end-of-training comparison.

gap: There is no seeded sequential-vs-parallel comparison anywhere below 1B, and PaLM's own 8B run shows a cost, so a 12-seed matched-token nano test would give the first estimate of the sign and size of the parallel penalty in the regime where it is expected to be largest.
notes: Prior is right and can be sharpened: the literature's small-scale support is one 1B single run (Falcon) plus an uncontrolled Pythia comparison. Parameter count is identical between the two block layouts, so matching is automatic; the confound to watch is that parallel blocks change the effective depth (first MLP sees raw embeddings), so report depth alongside. Investigating-FFN paper (arXiv:2305.13297) converts pretrained BERT/RoBERTa to parallel and is not a from-scratch test.

evidence.title: A Reproducibility Study of Partial Residual Ablations in Pre-LN Transformers (Babariya)
evidence.quote: training GPT-style models at 10M (TinyShakespeare) and 124M (OpenWebText) parameters ... removing the attention skip (FFNOnly configuration) causes deterministic collapse to the No-Residual floor across every seed and environment tested (mean 3.350 +/- 0.002, 3 seeds at 10M) ... a controlled 8-seed sweep ... gives mean 1.580 +/- 0.003 [AttnOnly] ... [Full residual 1.499-1.502; No Residual 3.356 at 10M/6 layers; 7.689 vs 3.263 at 124M/12 layers.]
evidence.what_it_shows: Seeded nano-scale evidence (6-layer, 10M, 3-8 seeds) that a plain stack with no residual sits at the collapse floor while the residual model trains; also that the attention skip is the load-bearing one. Short budget (3k steps) and char-level data, single-author preprint.

evidence.title: Deep Transformers without Shortcuts: Modifying Self-attention for Faithful Signal Propagation (He, Martens, Zhang, Botev, Brock, Smith, Teh)
evidence.quote: we show that it is possible to match the training loss of standard transformers with skipless ones by training for around 5 times longer [using E-SPA]; deep skipless transformers with standard attention suffer rank collapse and do not train.
evidence.what_it_shows: At depth, plain skipless transformers fail; they become trainable only with a modified attention/initialisation and then need ~5x the compute. Supports 'plain stacks do not train' while refuting 'residuals are strictly necessary'.

evidence.title: Cutting the Skip: Training Residual-Free Transformers (ICLR 2026)
evidence.quote: Plain skipless models with standard initialization: 61.4% ImageNet accuracy with AdamW versus 80.3% for the residual baseline; with the proposed Jacobian-based initialisation skipless ViTs reach parity. [12-layer ViT-B; depth ablations 9-12 layers; no seeds reported.]
evidence.what_it_shows: Vision, single-seed, 9-12 layers: same pattern, plain skipless collapses, principled init recovers it. No shallow (2-4 layer) runs.

evidence.title: Attention is Not All You Need: Pure Attention Loses Rank Doubly Exponentially with Depth (Dong, Cordonnier, Loukas)
evidence.quote: we find that pure attention decays in rank doubly exponentially with depth ... skip connections and MLPs are the two mechanisms that counteract this collapse.
evidence.what_it_shows: The mechanism: rank collapse grows with depth, so the failure is predicted to be depth-dependent and mild at 2-4 layers, which is the untested region.

gap: Nobody has run plain vs highway vs residual at 2 and 4 layers with seeds and a matched token budget: the seeded collapse result starts at 6 layers on a 3k-step char-level budget, so a 12-seed nano test would establish where the collapse depth threshold sits and whether highway gating (never run against transformers in this literature) recovers plain stacks.
notes: Prior is right on both halves: at >=6 layers plain stacks collapse (now with 8 seeds at 10M), at 2-4 layers it is untested and rank-collapse theory predicts the effect is small. 'Necessary' is false in the strict sense: E-SPA (He 2023) and Jacobian init (Cutting the Skip) train skipless stacks, so the claim to test is 'plain stacks with standard init and Pre-LN do not train'. Babariya's numbers also show the FFN skip can be dropped at 10M with a small cost (1.58 vs 1.50), which is a cheap extra arm.

evidence.title: MobileLLM: Optimizing Sub-billion Parameter Language Models for On-Device Use Cases (Liu et al.)
evidence.quote: In a 30-layer 125M model, sharing the input and output embeddings reduces the number of parameters by 16M (~11.8%) with a 0.2 points drop in average accuracy ... reallocating the saved parameters to add more layers (32 layers) gives a 0.4 points accuracy gain while still maintaining 10M fewer parameters. [No seeds or variance reported.]
evidence.what_it_shows: The closest thing to the proposed test: tied vs untied at ~125M, and tied-plus-reinvested at near-matched parameters, decoder LM. Single run; the 0.2-0.4 point deltas are inside typical seed noise on downstream averages.

evidence.title: Rethinking Embedding Coupling in Pre-trained Language Models (Chung, Fevry, Tsai, Johnson, Ruder; ICLR 2021)
evidence.quote: decoupled embeddings provide increased modeling flexibility ... by reallocating the input embedding parameters in the Transformer layers, we achieve dramatically better performance on standard natural language understanding tasks with the same number of parameters during fine-tuning.
evidence.what_it_shows: Matched-parameter evidence that untying (and shrinking the input embedding) wins, but for masked-LM encoders at BERT scale, multilingual, and measured after fine-tuning; not a decoder-LM loss comparison and no seeds reported.

evidence.title: Weight Tying Biases Token Embeddings Towards the Output Space
evidence.quote: we test only a single training run, as training runs at the billion-parameter scale are very costly, therefore we were not able to conduct statistical tests across multiple training runs, random seeds, etc. ... no consistent performance difference is observed [across eight benchmarks] ... At 70M parameters, embeddings account for 73.4% of the model, making weight tying highly impactful for parameter efficiency.
evidence.what_it_shows: Mechanism (output gradients dominate the shared matrix early, starving early layers) with unmatched, single-run billion-scale comparisons; says explicitly that tying's cost is representational and its benefit is the parameter saving that dominates at nano scale.

evidence.title: Using the Output Embedding to Improve Language Models (Press, Wolf)
evidence.quote: we show that tying the input and output embeddings ... improves perplexity on PTB and WikiText-2 while reducing the number of parameters. [LSTM language models; tied vs untied at the same d.]
evidence.what_it_shows: Origin: LSTM, small corpora, unmatched parameters (tying simply removes a matrix). No transformer, no seeds.

gap: No seeded, parameter-matched tied-vs-untied decoder comparison exists at any scale, and at 10-60M the embedding is 50-75% of the model so the reinvestment side (d or layers bought with the saved parameters) dominates the answer; a 12-seed matched test would give the first sign estimate with a variance bound in the regime where practitioners tie by default.
notes: Prior is right: transformer evidence is single-run (MobileLLM) or encoder-only (Chung). Large models untie for a stated reason now (2603.26663: gradient asymmetry, negligible savings above ~1B), so the 'nobody states with numbers' part of the prior is out of date. MobileLLM's reinvestment result (tied+2 layers beats untied at fewer params) is the version of the claim most worth testing; the raw tied-vs-untied-at-same-d comparison is not parameter-matched.

evidence.title: Scaling Laws with Vocabulary: Larger Models Deserve Larger Vocabularies (Tao et al.; NeurIPS 2024)
evidence.quote: training models ranging from 33M to 3B parameters on up to 500B characters with various vocabulary configurations ... the optimal vocabulary size depends on the compute budget, with larger models requiring larger vocabularies. [Body: vocabularies 4K-96K at fixed non-vocabulary parameters; unigram-normalised loss; 'an overly large vocabulary cannot be utilized efficiently, leading to sub-optimal model performance'; N_v^opt ∝ N_nv^0.83; Table 1 starts at 3B (37-43K); no seeds mentioned.]
evidence.what_it_shows: Controlled IsoFLOP grid showing an interior vocabulary optimum that grows with compute; extrapolating the fitted law puts the 33M optimum near the bottom of the 4K grid (~4-5K). Refutes 'at every scale' but matches non-vocabulary parameters, not total parameters, and reports no seeds.

evidence.title: Over-Tokenized Transformer: Vocabulary is Generally Worth Scaling (Huang et al.)
evidence.quote: we decouple input and output vocabularies ... scaling input vocabulary consistently improves performance across model sizes with a log-linear relationship, at negligible cost, while scaling the output vocabulary does not.
evidence.what_it_shows: The controlled evidence on the other side: for the input embedding only, larger is monotonically better at all scales tested. The claim is therefore true for the input table and false for the output head, which is the Tao result.

evidence.title: The Languini Kitchen: Enabling Language Modelling Research at Different Scales of Compute (Stanic et al.)
evidence.quote: [GPT tiny, 53.9M parameters, 138k steps, seven vocabularies from 2,048 to 131,072, normalised perplexity:] Increasing the size of the vocabulary improves performance but has diminishing gains and significantly slow down the model ... a 16k and 32k vocabulary strikes a good balance.
evidence.what_it_shows: A nano-scale sweep at fixed steps (not matched bytes or parameters) with a byte-normalised metric: gains flatten by 16-32K. Single run, and the embedding parameters are not counted against the budget.

gap: Neither Tao (matches non-vocabulary parameters) nor Languini (matches steps) counts the embedding against the budget or reports seeds, so a 12-seed test at matched total parameters and matched bytes, scored in bits per byte, would show whether the nano-scale optimum is really ~4K or whether the unpaid embedding parameters are what made small vocabularies look best.
notes: Prior is right (Tao: small models want small output vocabularies) but incomplete: Over-Tokenized shows input-vocabulary scaling is free at every scale, so the test must separate the input table from the output head or it will average two opposite effects. Tao compares with unigram-normalised loss; bits per byte is cleaner and is what the brief proposes.

evidence.title: Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models (Muennighoff et al.; NeurIPS 2023, JMLR 2025)
evidence.quote: we run a large set of experiments varying the extent of data repetition and compute budget, ranging up to 900 billion training tokens and 9 billion parameter models. We find that with constrained data for a fixed compute budget, training with up to 4 epochs of repeated data yields negligible changes to loss compared to having unique data. [Body: 'the N=8.7 billion parameter model trained for four epochs finishes training with only 0.5% higher validation loss than the single-epoch model'; seeds (5) reported only for the code/filter augmentation figures.]
evidence.what_it_shows: The source of the four-epoch figure: 400 single-seed runs, the headline number measured at 8.7B, the fitted law's repeated-token decay parameter assumed size-independent. Not replicated below ~100M with seeds.

evidence.title: To Repeat or Not To Repeat: Insights from Scaling LLM under Token-Crisis (Xue et al.; NeurIPS 2023)
evidence.quote: we empirically investigate repeating pre-training data for additional epochs ... the model is susceptible to overfitting, leading to multi-epoch degradation ... significant factors include dataset size, model parameters, and training objectives. [T5-Base 247M to T5-XL 2.8B; C4 subsets repeated up to 256 epochs; 5-run std for downstream evals.]
evidence.what_it_shows: Independent confirmation at 247M-2.8B that heavy repetition degrades, that larger models degrade more, and that dropout is the one regulariser that rescues it. Encoder-decoder, extreme epoch counts, no nano scale.

evidence.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data (Hernandez et al.)
evidence.quote: performance of an 800M parameter model can be degraded to that of a 2x smaller model (400M params) by repeating 0.1% of the data 100 times, despite the other 90% of the training tokens remaining unique.
evidence.what_it_shows: Repetition of a subset harms non-monotonically (double descent); establishes that 'epochs' is not the only knob and that the harm peaks at moderate repeat counts.

evidence.title: Train Smarter, Not Longer: Memorization-Guided Data Reuse for Efficient LLM Training
evidence.quote: Our preliminary experiments reveal a consistent memorization-driven regime: performance continues to improve with repetition far beyond current practice (e.g., the commonly cited four-epoch limit).
evidence.what_it_shows: A workshop preprint contesting the four-epoch knee for downstream metrics; preliminary, sizes and seeds not stated. Enough to say the number is quoted more confidently than it is measured.

gap: The four-epoch knee is a single-seed measurement at 8.7B plus a fitted law whose repeat-decay term is assumed independent of model size, so a 12-seed 1-32 epoch sweep at matched steps on 10-60M models would be the first direct test of whether the knee is scale-invariant and how wide it is relative to seed variance.
notes: Prior is right: 'four' is a rounding of 'negligible to ~4, decaying, near-worthless by ~40' and comes from >1B runs. Muennighoff's 5-seed panels exist but only for the code/filter experiments, not the epoch sweep. Design note: hold the unique-token slice fixed and vary steps (their protocol) or hold steps fixed and vary the slice (ours); the two answer different questions and the four-epoch figure belongs to the first.

evidence.title: Curriculum Learning for Language Modeling (Campos)
